Title: Integrating image processing and machine learning for phase specific estimation of Manning roughness coefficient in furrow irrigation
Text:
Integrating image processing and 
machine learning for phase specific 
estimation of Manning roughness 
coefficient in furrow irrigation
Hadi Rezaei Rad1,2, Hamed Ebrahimian2, Abdolmajid Liaghat2, Mahmoud Omid3, 
Fatemeh Khalaji2 & Mahshid Shabani Arani2
Accurate estimation of Manning’s roughness coefficient (n) is vital for hydrological modeling and 
optimizing furrow irrigation systems, yet traditional methods remain limited due to spatial-temporal 
variability, the need for expert users, the inherent limitations of hydraulic equations, and labor-
intensive measurements. This study introduces a novel algorithm that integrates high-resolution 
image processing with machine learning techniques to dynamically predict n during advance and 
storage phases in bare furrows. Three scenarios were evaluated: (i) full-field data (including inflow/
outflow rates, advance/recession times, infiltration, slope, soil moisture, furrow images and etc.), (ii) 
images only, and (iii) images plus selected field data (inflow rate, slope, cross-sectional area, clod size 
and irrigation events). Manning’s n was computed using the SIPAR_ID model and Manning’s equation 
in advance and storage phases, yielding ranges of 0.017–0.636 (advance phase) and 0.015–0.317 
(storage phase), with respective means of 0.083 and 0.054. The Random Forest algorithm in Scenario (i) 
achieved near-perfect performance (99% precision, recall, and F1-score), while Scenario (iii) preserved 
95–96% accuracy with significantly reduced data inputs. Notably, excluding hydraulic variables 
(Scenario ii) led to a ~ 50% performance drop, highlighting their importance. This approach offers a 
robust, cost-effective solution for n estimation, bridging the gap between precision, practicality, and 
real-time application in sustainable water management and precision agriculture.

Effective water management in furrow irrigation systems depends on various factors, including the inflow rate, 
soil type, furrow slope, infiltration rate, crop type, surface roughness of the furrows, and irrigation method 
used1. Among these factors, roughness is of particular interest because of its spatial and temporal heterogeneity 
and its critical role in surface irrigation simulation models2–4. Various coefficients, such as Chezy, Manning, and 
Darcy, are commonly used to interpret roughness, each represented as a constant in their respective equations. 
Among these equations, the Manning equation (Eq. (1)) has been widely accepted by hydraulic and irrigation 
engineers for modeling flow in open channels and surface irrigation systems, for the most part, because it is 
simple and quite accurate in predicting roughness5.
Nonetheless, the use of this equation in surface irrigation, especially in furrow irrigation, has various 
limitations because of its foundational assumption. First, the Manning equation assumes steady and uniform 
flow6,7, meaning that the flow remains constant over time and that the cross-sectional area of the flow (Aflow) 
does not vary along the flow path. In contrast, in irrigation furrows, the flow is often unsteady and nonuniform 
due to water infiltration and changes in furrow shape8. Second, the Manning equation assumes a prismatic flow 
cross-Sects9–11. , whereas furrow irrigation typically involves nonprismatic cross-sections caused by plowing and 
the presence of clods. Additionally, the Manning equation is designed primarily for deep flows, making its use 
questionable in shallow surface irrigation, where flow characteristics vary significantly due to bed roughness8,12.

Despite these limitations, the Manning equation is still widely used because of its simplicity and the absence 
of better alternatives. It is generally applied to describe flow conditions in surface irrigation once infiltration 
stabilizes (i.e., reaches the basic infiltration rate), which typically occurs during the storage phase5,13. However, 
in other irrigation phases, such as the advance phase, where infiltration into the soil remains unstable and 
determining the flow depth, Aflow, and wetted perimeter (Pw) becomes nearly impossible, the accuracy of 
the Manning equation becomes even more uncertain. Therefore, applying the Manning equation to estimate 
the roughness coefficient during these phases may lead to unreliable results. To overcome these limitations, 
alternative methods and assumptions that allow for a more accurate estimation of the roughness coefficient are 
needed.
Numerous methodologies have been proposed for estimating Manning’s n, which are classified into five 
main categories: image-based methods, empirical tables, empirical relations, direct methods, and analytical or 
inverse solutions. Some of these methods have facilitated the creation of computer models such as SIPAR_ID 
14, EVALUE15, and SIRMOD16, which simulate surface irrigation flow and estimate infiltration parameters and 
roughness coefficients. Other methods rely on analytical approaches or direct application of the Manning Eqs. 
17–19. A review of several studies1,2,12,19–23 revealed that estimating Manning’s n requires extensive field data 
collection, making the process time-consuming and costly. This often leads to treating the roughness coefficient 
as a constant value via empirical tables and relations, despite the potential for significant estimation errors23. 
However, over- or underestimating the Manning roughness coefficient can cause substantial errors in surface 
irrigation design and simulation24. Focusing on changes in the roughness coefficient throughout irrigation 
is highly important for better understanding irrigation dynamics. Employing simplified approaches and 
assumptions is recommended to reduce the complexity of roughness estimation.
Machine vision systems, which utilize image processing and machine learning techniques, offer promising 
alternatives. These systems are widely used across industries and are increasingly applied in the agricultural 
sciences25. In these systems, various features are first extracted from images via image processing techniques. In 
the next step, a relationship is established between these features and the values of the investigated parameter 
by applying machine learning methods (such as logistic regression (LR)26, linear discriminant analysis (LDA)27, 
k-nearest neighbor (KNN)28, decision trees (CART)29, random forest (RF)30, support vector machine (SVM)31, 
multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural networks32, and simple Bayesian (NBGaussian)33, allowing for the 
estimation of the desired parameter on the basis of the extracted relationship.
These techniques enable the extraction of useful information, such as plant size and number34, soil moisture 
and infiltration rates35–37, surface cracks38,39, and soil characteristics40–42. Given that the integration of machine 
learning and image processing techniques has proven successful in detecting clod size and number, soil type, 
surface roughness, and other related features, these techniques can likely also be effectively applied to estimate 
the Manning roughness coefficient. This is particularly relevant since the Manning roughness coefficient is 
affected by many of these parameters, either directly or indirectly.
In light of the challenges associated with the accurate estimation of Manning’s roughness coefficient (n) in 
furrow irrigation- particularly its spatial and temporal variability- this study addresses a significant knowledge 
gap in current methodologies. Traditional approaches often rely on expert judgment, empirical observations, 
and time-consuming field measurements, which limit their repeatability and practicality under varying field 
conditions. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel framework that integrates high-resolution soil surface 
images and field-measured hydraulic parameters via image processing and machine learning techniques. 
The scientific contribution of this work lies in presenting a dynamic, data-driven, and practical method for 
estimating Manning’s n that enables faster, more accessible, and repeatable assessments without requiring 
advanced technical expertise or specialized instruments. This research hypothesizes that the simultaneous use 
of image processing and machine learning techniques can accurately estimate Manning’s n in furrow irrigation 
during both the advance and storage phases. Specifically, it is hypothesized that the Manning equation can 
be applied during the storage phase, whereas the SIPAR_ID model, which uses input velocity and flow depth 
data at specific points in time during the advance phase14, can be used for estimation in that phase. The main 
goal of this study was to assess the performance of the proposed method in Manning’s n estimation in furrow 
irrigation, during both the advance and storage phases. Certain variables (such as vegetation cover) that could 
complicate data collection and factors varying light conditions during imaging were eliminated to simplify the 
data collection and algorithm training process. Thus, bare furrows under consistent lighting conditions were 
used for the analysis. We assessed the performance of image processing and machine learning methods by 
averaging image data, field data, and hydraulic data both separately and in combination. In the next step, after 
the effectiveness of the developed algorithm was validated, various machine learning techniques (such as LR, 
LDA, KNN, CART, RF, SVM, MLP, and NBGaussian) were used to evaluate the accuracy of roughness coefficient 
estimation, across different scenarios, each considering a varying number of input data. The most significant 
scientific achievement of this study is the introduction of image processing and machine learning as a dynamic 
approach for estimating Manning’s n in furrow irrigation, capturing both temporal and spatial variations for the 
first time under various field conditions.
Materials and methods
Field experiments
The pilot fields were established at the University of Tehran’s experimental farm in Karaj, with geographic 
coordinates of 50°57’30.2” E and 35°48’18.5” N, where the annual average rainfall is 251 mm. The study was 
conducted on two experimental fields with distinct soil textures: silty clay loam and clay loam. The first field, 
designated Field F, has been under continuous cultivation for many years. In contrast, the second field, designated 
Field E, had remained fallow for several years. The physical and chemical properties of the soils from both fields 
are presented in Table 1.

This study aimed to explore the influence of key factors on Manning’s n, an essential parameter in surface 
irrigation. The research analyzed six different inflow rates, representing various furrow conditions and the 
maximum nonerosive rate. Furthermore, the study considered the effects of three irrigation events and their 
distinct phases: the advance phase, which covers the time water takes to travel from the field’s entrance to its 
end, and the storage phase, which spans from the completion of the advance phase until the cessation of water 
flow. In addition, this research examined how irrigation intervals (5-day vs. 10-day) and soil textures (Fields E 
and F) affect Manning’s roughness coefficient. These parameters were quantified through image-derived texture 
analysis and integrated into machine learning models as categorical variables, improving roughness prediction 
accuracy. The Field E experiments involved three low inflow rates (0.27 L/s) and three high inflow rates (0.57 L/s) 
at both intervals. Similar tests were conducted in field F, but the 10-day interval included six low and six high 
inflow rates to enhance the algorithm’s learning process. Data collection limitations prevented further expansion 
in Field E (due to the labor-intensive and costly nature of data collection). Overall, during the three events, 90 
furrows were analyzed, 18 of which were in Field F and 12 of which were in Field E. The advance and storage 
phases were analyzed separately because of their critical influence on Manning’s n.
Upstream of the field, a tank with a volume of 2000 L was placed to mitigate fluctuations in water pressure 
and to allow water to flow by gravity, and the water was transferred to the experimental furrows by polyethylene 
pipes (two pipes with a diameter and a length of 40 mm and 35 m, respectively). In both fields, furrows with 
widths of 75 cm and lengths of 20 m were created (the length was considered as short as possible so that the 
images taken from the surface of the furrow would be a good representation of the overall condition of the 
furrow). Among these furrows, 10 stations in the furrow at a distance of 2 m from each other were considered 
to measure the advance and recession times. Type 2 Washington State College (WSC) flumes43 were installed at 
both the inlet and outlet of each furrow to measure the inflow and outflow rates (Fig. 1). The water depth in the 
flumes was recorded every five minutes during the first hour and then at ten-minute intervals until the irrigation 
process was completed. Four rulers were placed along the furrows at 4-meter intervals to measure the water 
depth during irrigation, providing the data necessary to calculate the energy gradient, cross-sectional area, and 
wetted perimeter of the flow. All the furrows were irrigated for approximately 180 min.
Given that, for furrows longer than 40 ft (12.2 m), the bed slope can be used in place of the energy gradient44 
- a substitution justified by hydraulic equivalence under uniform flow conditions where gravitational forces 
balance boundary friction- the bed slope of the furrows was determined and applied (Tables 2 and 3). This 
substitution maintains engineering accuracy when flow remains subcritical and channel geometry is consistent, 
conditions satisfied in the experimental setup.
Before irrigation, the soil moisture content was assessed via the gravimetric method. From each furrow, three 
samples were collected from the topsoil layer (0–10 cm), and the average moisture content was then calculated 
for further analysis.
The cross-sectional area (Af) of each furrow was assessed with a profile meter45 at three predetermined 
points: the upstream Sect. (2 m from the starting point), the middle Sect. (10 m from the starting point), and 
the downstream Sect. (18 m from the starting point). These measurements were taken before and after each 
irrigation event via a profile meter. Furthermore, the flow cross-sectional area (Aflow) and wetted perimeter (Pw) 
were calculated by determining the flow depth at different intervals with rulers and a profile meter. The average 
values for both the cross-sectional area and wetted perimeter were documented before and after irrigation, and 
these values were utilized in later analyses46.
A summary of the data collected from the experimental furrows in both fields is provided in Tables 2 and 3.
Determination of manning roughness coefficient
Manning’s n was independently calculated for each examined phase, and the method used to determine the 
roughness coefficient in these phases is detailed below:
Advance phase
Given the assumption of the Manning equation, its application in irrigation is not appropriate. This is due to 
infiltration during irrigation, which leads to a reduction in the flow cross-sectional area and, consequently, 
causes flow nonuniformity, making the equation unsuitable for such scenarios. However, owing to the lack of 
a suitable and practical equation and the simplicity of calculations, researchers use this relationship to explain 
the hydraulic conditions of surface irrigation flow after water infiltration stabilizes in the soil (reaching the basic 
infiltration rate).

Rather than directly applying Manning’s equation, this study employs the SIPAR_ID model to estimate 
Manning’s n as an effective hydraulic resistance coefficient during the advance phase. This coefficient encapsulates 
the combined influence of bed roughness and transient flow conditions, enabling practical simulation of advance-
phase hydraulics even under deviations from the equation’s theoretical assumptions. Despite the absence of 
a theoretically superior alternative, Manning’s n remains a pragmatic and widely communicable metric for 
characterizing hydraulic resistance in transient scenarios. The SIPAR_ID model was selected for its proven 
capacity to simultaneously calibrate infiltration and resistance parameters using field-measured advance-phase 
data, as demonstrated in prior studies46–48. In this model, the input consists of advance phase data, together 
with the inflow rate and flow depth at a given location and at multiple time points, to evaluate the infiltration 
parameters and Manning roughness coefficient14. Thus, it is likely useful for the estimation of Manning’s n in the 
advance phase. In this study, inflow rates and flow depth data were input into the model from the beginning of 
irrigation to the conclusion of the advance phase, allowing for the estimation of infiltration parameters and the 
Manning roughness coefficient throughout the phase.

Storage phase
When water is delivered to the furrow’s end, the storage phase begins and continues until the inflow stops. 
Almost one hour after irrigation began, the water infiltration rate into the soil leveled off, and the outflow from 
the furrows, which had a steady inflow, also became uniform. This finding indicates that sufficient time was 
available for infiltration in all furrows after the steady inflow reached the base infiltration rate (Tables 2 and 3). 
By the end of this period, uniform flow conditions were achieved along the furrow. Using Manning’s equation 
(Eq. (1)), the storage period was determined as the duration from when the base infiltration rate was established 
until the irrigation cutoff was reached.

Image preparation
To estimate the Manning roughness coefficient, images were taken from the surface of irrigation furrows via a 
Canon PowerShot SX540 HS digital camera with a 20-megapixel sensor and a maximum image size (resolution) 
of 3888 × 5184. To cover the entire considered surface properly and stabilize the photography and lighting 
conditions in all the furrows, a cart with a height of one meter was made. The standardized imaging protocol 
in this study was intentionally adopted to isolate the algorithm’s core performance from confounding variables 
during development. In this study, 90 furrows were examined, and images of 9 specific points (at distances of 
2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16 m from the beginning of the furrow) in each furrow were taken during two phases: 
advance and recession of irrigation. Therefore, a total of 1620 images were collected. A total of 1486 images were 
considered for the training and testing process after the noisy images and the images related to the furrows with 
missing data were removed (Tables 2 and 3). After that, 80% of the images were used for training (1190 images), 
and the remaining 20% of the images were used for testing (296 images).

In addition to flow rate, initial soil moisture, and soil texture, other parameters, such as clod size and number, 
also impact the flow velocity in furrows, which in turn affects the Manning roughness coefficient. Although 
it is challenging to quantify the size and number of clods, an effort was made to consider the influence of this 
parameter as much as possible in the developed algorithm by defining indicators.
In addition, the flow rate, initial soil moisture, soil texture, and other parameters, such as the size and number 
of clods, influence the flow velocity in the furrow and consequently the Manning roughness coefficient. This is 
because it is difficult to determine the size and number of clods quantitatively; therefore, an effort was made to

Development of an algorithm for roughness coefficient determination
After collecting field data, preparing images, and determining Manning’s n, the images were analyzed via the 
Python programming language. A set of features was extracted from the images, and the effectiveness of different 
machine learning methods in classifying roughness was evaluated. Therefore, 80% of the images were used for 
training (1190 images), and 20% of the images were used for testing (296 images).
Feature extraction
Feature extraction is crucial in simplifying the extensive data contained within images by identifying essential 
patterns or attributes. This significantly aids in processes such as classification, segmentation, and modeling49. 
Effective feature extraction not only reduces the dimensionality of the data but also enhances the performance 
of predictive models and analytical algorithms50.
Different features in three ranges related to shape and size, texture and color were extracted from the images 
taken from the surface of the furrows (Fig. 3). For this purpose, seven features related to shape and size were 
extracted by using a statistical torque called Hu’s momentum51. Moreover, using the co-occurrence matrix 
method52 and the local binary pattern (LBP)53, which have been widely used by other scholars54–57, 16 and 156 
textural features were extracted from the images, respectively. Finally, 512 color features were prepared via the 
HSV color space and its normalized histogram.
Examined scenarios
The Manning roughness coefficient depends on various factors, including soil characteristics, hydraulic flow 
conditions, and other related variables. Failing to consider any of these factors can introduce errors in estimating 
Manning’s n. In this study, the goal was to evaluate the efficiency of using image processing techniques combined 
with machine learning methods to estimate Manning’s n in furrow irrigation. For this purpose, it is crucial to 
provide an algorithm with all the parameters that influence the roughness coefficient as inputs to allow accurate 
estimation. Some of these features, such as soil bed roughness, the presence or absence of clods, and soil 
moisture, are visible in surface soil images. However, certain hydraulic features, such as flow velocity and cross-
sectional area, are not detectable in the images. Therefore, in addition to images, it is likely that both hydraulic 
and nonhydraulic parameters must be provided to the algorithm for accurate estimation. To achieve this goal, 
various scenarios were defined to assess the algorithm using different sets of data.
The first scenario was designed to incorporate all hydraulic and nonhydraulic data collected in the field, along 
with furrow surface images. This approach allowed for training the algorithm with the largest available dataset 
and determining the highest possible accuracy.
Since determining some parameters in the first scenario was time-consuming or expensive (such as the flow 
cross-section, advance time, recession time, etc.), these parameters were excluded from the learning process 
for other scenarios. In the next step, another scenario was defined to evaluate the algorithm’s performance 
solely on the basis of images. Other scenarios, such as using images and hydraulic parameters, using images 
and nonhydraulic parameters, and using hydraulic and nonhydraulic parameters without images, were also 
examined. However, owing to the algorithm’s low efficiency in certain cases, the results of these investigations 
were not presented.
Finally, the accuracy of the developed algorithm was checked in each of the three selected scenarios to 
determine the best approach. A scenario in which the algorithm with the least amount of input data achieves the 
highest accuracy in estimating the roughness coefficient is selected. The scenarios are as follows:
The first scenario uses images and all measured field data, which include images plus the inflow rate, outflow 
rate, advance time, recession time, infiltrated water volume, irrigation event number, initial soil moisture, slope, 
final (basic) infiltration rate, index of size and number of clods before and after irrigation, electrical conductivity 
(EC) and pH of the soil, cross-sectional area of the furrow, cross-sectional area of the flow and wetted perimeter.
The second scenario uses only images taken from the surface of the furrows.

Categorization
The Manning roughness coefficient is a continuous parameter and depends on various factors. The change in 
each of these factors can lead to a change in its value, which makes it difficult to estimate the roughness coefficient 
via machine vision. Therefore, in this study, for convenience, the roughness coefficient was categorized into 
different classes. For this purpose, the roughness coefficients before irrigation (roughness coefficient in the 
advance phase) were sorted from low to high, and the roughness values were placed in the positive and negative 
ranges of 10% in one group (class). Similarly, the roughness coefficients after irrigation (roughness coefficient in 
the storage phase) were also divided into different groups. Accordingly, the roughness coefficients after irrigation 
were classified into nine classes (0–8), and those before irrigation were classified into ten classes (9–18) (Table 4).
According to the classification, if the algorithm correctly recognizes the class of each furrow, it is able to 
estimate the Manning roughness coefficient with a maximum error margin of 10%.

Below is a summary of several commonly utilized methods across various domains, emphasizing their features, 
advantages, and drawbacks.
Naive Bayes (NB)  The naive Bayes algorithm is grounded in Bayes’ theorem and operates under the presump­
tion that all the features are independent of one another60. Although this assumption may not always be accurate, 
naive Bayes is still effective, especially in applications such as text classification and spam detection60. It performs 
well in situations where datasets are noisy and only limited training data are available, as it can generate reliable 
predictions even with minimal data61. However, the independence assumption can result in less-than-optimal 
performance when significant correlations exist among features. Various adaptations, including Gaussian, mul­
tinomial, complement, Bernoulli, and categorical models, have been developed for different data types59.
Linear discriminant analysis (LDA)  LDA is a simple classifier that reduces data dimensions, increasing com­
putational efficiency (particularly for high-dimensional datasets)62. It assumes that the data follow a normal dis­
tribution with equal covariance matrices across classes. While this makes LDA appropriate for linearly separable 
datasets, its effectiveness diminishes when the homoscedasticity assumption is not met. LDA is often compared 
with ANOVA and regression techniques because of their common statistical foundations.
Logistic regression (LR)  Logistic regression is a widely utilized probabilistic model for binary classification 
that estimates outcome probabilities by fitting data to a logistic or sigmoid function63. One drawback of logistic 
regression (LR) is its reliance on the assumption of a straightforward linear relationship between independent 
variables and the log-odds of the dependent variable. This assumption may not be valid for more complex data­
sets. Regularization methods such as L1 and L2 are frequently used to prevent overfitting in high-dimensional 
datasets62.
K-nearest neighbors (KNN)  The K-nearest neighbor (KNN) algorithm is a nonparametric method that assigns 
data points to a class by considering the majority class among their closest neighbors64. Its implementation is 
straightforward, and it works well for nonlinear decision boundaries. However, its performance heavily relies 
on the selection of ‘k’ (the number of neighbors) and the distance metric used. Additionally, KNN can become 
computationally intensive for large datasets since it requires storing all instances during prediction62.
Support vector machine (SVM)  SVM creates a hyperplane to differentiate classes in high-dimensional space, 
which is functional for both linear and nonlinear classification tasks, particularly when utilizing kernel functions 
such as polynomials, radial basis functions (RBFs), and sigmoid kernels. While SVMs are generally robust, they 
may struggle with noisy datasets where class boundaries overlap65. Careful selection of kernels and hyperparam­
eters is essential for achieving optimal results.
Decision tree (DT)  Decision trees represent intuitive and easily interpretable methodologies for classification 
tasks and regression tasks. Data are divided through a recursive process of partitioning feature values, resulting 
in a tree-like structure of decisions29. However, decision trees are prone to overfitting, especially in noisy da­
tasets. Techniques such as pruning have been developed to streamline tree structures and enhance generaliza­
tion66. Recent developments, particularly in analysis, have broadened the scope of decision trees67,68.
Random forest (RF)  Random Forest is a machine learning technique that builds multiple decision trees during 
training and combines their outputs to improve accuracy while minimizing overfitting. 30. By utilizing bagging 
(bootstrap aggregation) and random feature selection, the RF promotes diversity among its decision trees, re­
sulting in more robust predictions69,70. However, as the number of trees increases, RFs can become computa­
tionally demanding62.
Multilayer perceptron (MLP)  An MLP is a deep learning architecture composed of several layers of neurons. 
It employs backpropagation to modify the weights of connections between neurons, allowing it to learn intricate 
patterns within data58. The MLP is capable of modeling nonlinear relationships but necessitates careful tuning 
of hyperparameters, including the number of layers, neurons, and iterations. Moreover, it is sensitive to feature 
scaling and may require significant computational resources when processing large datasets59.
In this study, the effectiveness of these classification techniques for predicting Manning’s roughness coefficient 
was assessed. Given the time-consuming and expensive nature of field data collection, compiling a large dataset 
was impractical. To evaluate the accuracy of these algorithms, a cross-validation approach was implemented to 
ensure thorough training and testing.
Cross-validation is a statistical technique employed to assess and compare learning algorithms by partitioning 
the data: the first subset is utilized for training or developing the model, whereas the other subset serves to 
validate the model’s performance. In k-fold cross-validation, the dataset is initially divided into k equally sized 
subsets or folds. Following this division, the process undergoes k iterations of training and validation. In each 
iteration, a unique subset is reserved for validation, while the remaining k-1 subsets are utilized for training the 
model. 71,72.
Finally, the average of these k validation times is chosen as the final estimate. In this research, the value of 
K was set to 10. Given that the training and testing process is reiterated K times and the average results are 
presented, training and testing have the necessary validity, and there is no need to perform algorithm evaluation 
operations using validation data.

Results and discussion
Manning roughness coefficient values
The results obtained from Tables 5 and 6 reveal valuable insights into the hydraulic behavior of furrow irrigation 
in Fields E and F. Specifically, Manning’s roughness coefficient (n) was estimated for both the advance and 
storage phases, whereas the accuracy of the SIPAR_ID model in simulating the advance phase was carefully 
evaluated.
In terms of model performance, SIPAR_ID demonstrated remarkable accuracy. The coefficient of 
determination (R²) ranged from 0.91 to 0.999 in Field E and from 0.98 to 1.00 in Field F, indicating a near-
perfect match between the observed and simulated advance times. The Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) varied 
between 0.2 and 2.6 min in Field E and between 0.08 and 0.8 min in Field F. The relative error (RE) also remained 
within acceptable bounds, ranging from 0.29% to 10.8% in Field E and from 0.9% to 12.4% in Field F. Averaging 
across both fields, the R² reached 0.995, with an RMSE of just 0.363 min and an RE of 4.2%, clearly highlighting 
the robustness and precision of the SIPAR_ID model in predicting Manning roughness under varying field 
conditions.
These findings align closely with the results reported by Nie et al. (2014, 2018) and Ramezani Etedali et al. 
(2011), confirming that the SIPAR_ID model is a reliable tool for simulating surface irrigation hydraulics47,48,75. 
Looking deeper into the hydraulic resistance behavior, the average Manning’s n values during the advance and 
storage phases in Field E were found to be 0.110 and 0.073, respectively. In Field F, the corresponding values 
were 0.064 and 0.041. These results clearly show that as the number of irrigation events increased, the roughness 
coefficient consistently decreased in both phases. This behavior is consistent with previous studies by Bahmani 
et al. (2020) and Zarakani et al. (2020), and it emphasizes the dynamic nature of hydraulic roughness in response 
to repeated irrigation76,77. The underlying cause of this reduction in roughness is closely tied to soil surface 
transformations triggered by wetting and drying cycles between irrigation events. As shown in Fig. 4, these 
cycles contribute to the gradual disintegration of clods and smoothing of the soil surface. With time, the soil 
becomes more compacted and less resistant to water flow, thus decreasing Manning’s n value. This observation is 
not only supported by field measurements but also theoretically grounded in earlier works by Amiri et al. (2016), 
Harun-ur-Rashid (1990), Kassem & Ghonimy (2011), who emphasized the sensitivity of hydraulic roughness to 
soil moisture regimes and structural changes1,17,79.

First, the best method for estimating the roughness classifications was determined; then, by using 80% of the 
data for training, the random forest method was employed to develop the algorithm, with the remaining 20% set 
aside for testing purposes. The results are presented in Table 8. The average values of the precision, recall and F1-
score indices for this classification method were the same and equal to 99%, which indicates the high accuracy 
of the random forest classifier in detecting different classes of the Manning roughness coefficient. The superior 
performance of Random Forest aligns with its well-documented capacity to process complex datasets while 
minimizing overfitting through ensemble-based learning80. Unlike conventional linear approaches, this method 
excels at modeling nonlinear feature dependencies (a critical advantage for hydraulic roughness estimation). 
Field-collected data, which inherently contain measurement noise and variability, were handled more reliably 
by Random Forest compared to both k-nearest neighbors and single decision trees30. While support vector 
machines demonstrated moderate accuracy in preliminary tests, their computational demands and sensitivity to 
parameter tuning reduced their practical utility for this application81. An important characteristic of RF is that it 
is relatively resistant to overfitting problems35,82, which makes the algorithm resistant to errors caused by noisy 
data. According to the results, except for classes 4, 7, 12 and 13, the other classes were classified correctly with 
100% accuracy.
The confusion matrix for the random forest method in the first scenario is displayed in Table 9. The results 
revealed that, except for class 7, in which 3 of the 21 data points were classified in the incorrect class (class 4), no 
incorrect classification was observed in the other classes. Table 10 shows an example of the images of classes 4 and 
7. Classes 4 and 7 are both related to the storage phase (i.e., the furrows are wet); hence, the algorithm correctly 
separates the storage and advance phases. As shown in Table 10 (i.e., the images), the furrow bed in class 4 (e.g., 
F10-1-7) appears smoother than that in class 7 (e.g., E10-1-3). It was expected that the algorithm would correctly 
recognize this difference and provide an accurate classification. However, the inclusion of field data in network 
training means that the difference in substrates is not the sole factor influencing the selection of the roughness 
class. In fact, the complexity of analyzing the field images and data caused the algorithm to encounter difficulties 
in classifying some cases. It is difficult to find the cause of this incorrect classification simply by examining 
the images of the classes. It is also difficult to find the exact cause due to many complexities and, of course, 
the nature of machine learning methods, which act as black boxes83. Moreover, inaccurate estimation of the 
Manning roughness coefficient may also cause inaccurate training of the algorithm and, consequently, incorrect 
classification. The inaccurate estimation of the Manning roughness coefficient may stem from uncertainties 
associated with the inverse solution of the equations employed in this study for roughness coefficient estimation. 
Consequently, multiple estimations with varying parameter values may yield identical results in the inverse 
solution process.
In addition to class 7, in class 12, out of the total of 16 test data, the algorithm classified 2 data points in the 
wrong class and placed them in class 13 (Table 9). In this class, the algorithm correctly recognized the irrigation 
phase and was able to classify the roughness coefficient in the desired class with good accuracy (Table 10). In 
this class, according to Table 11, the visual difference that can be analyzed by the human eye is not visible, and 
no specific reason can be mentioned for this incorrect classification (e.g., F10-1-3 and F10-3-4 have different 
roughness values, but their images are very similar). Notably, owing to the great similarity of the images taken 
from the furrow surface, this amount of error might be sensible, although the field data collection greatly helped 
to reduce this error.
Finally, if all the data collected from the field and the images were used simultaneously, the model would 
classify the roughness coefficient values with an appropriate accuracy. However, since the determination of some 
input values to the model, such as the flow cross-sectional area and wetted perimeter, is time-consuming and 
difficult, using this scenario for roughness estimation is not desirable.

Third scenario
The validation results for all ten experimental folds revealed that the RF method, with values of the precision, 
accuracy and recall indices equal to 85, 88 and 85%, and the CART method, with values of these indices equal to 
85, 86 and 85%, had the most suitable performance (Table 7).
By training and testing the RF and CART methods, which yielded the best results, the CART method 
provided the most accurate data classification, with average precision, recall and F1-score indices of 95%, 96% 
and 95%, respectively, in all 19 classes (Table 14). These results revealed that other field parameters, such as the 
flow cross-sectional area and wetted perimeter, salinity, acidity, initial soil moisture, index of size and number 
of clods after irrigation (and other parameters not considered compared with those in the first scenario), are 
of relatively low importance and can be neglected to speed up the estimation and classification of roughness 
samples. Moreover, measuring these parameters in the field is difficult and time-consuming, and ignoring them 
leads to a reduction in the cost and time required for data collection. The indicators showed that the efficiency 
of the algorithm in classifying samples decreased slightly (approximately 3–4%) compared with that of the first 
scenario, which can be ignored owing to the increase in the speed of data collection and the implementation of 
the algorithm and the ability to obtain the results.
In addition to the high performance under limited data conditions (Scenario III), the algorithm’s ability to 
estimate Manning’s n dynamically (considering phase-specific variations) marks a significant improvement over 
static or constant approaches traditionally used in furrow irrigation models.
Table 15 shows the confusion matrix of the CART method in the classification of roughness samples. The 
results revealed that the classification of classes 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 13 and 16 was associated with errors in some samples. 
The algorithm classified 30 samples in class 13 out of a total of 35 samples, one sample in class 14, one sample 
in class 4, one sample in class 3 and two samples in class zero, which indicates that the distribution of incorrect 
classifications is greater than that of other classes.
Table 16 shows a sample of the images taken from the furrows in class 13 and other classes in which the 
sample of class 13 is incorrectly classified. In class 13, the algorithm failed to recognize the correct irrigation 
phase, and except for the samples classified in class 14 (samples F5-2-6 and F10-3-8), the other samples in the 
incorrect class were placed in the class with a storage phase; that is, class 13 was related to the advance phase and 
dry furrows. The algorithm classified 4 out of 35 tested samples in classes with a storage phase (e.g., E5-2-3 (class 
13) and E5-2-2 (class 0)). In contrast, this type of classification was also observed in class 7. In other misclassified 
classes, the irrigation phase has been correctly detected. The cause of this type of misclassification is not clear 
owing to the complexity of the algorithm, but as mentioned earlier, the influence of uncertainty in estimating the 
Manning roughness coefficient and the occurrence of such errors cannot be ignored.

lighting and fixed camera height—the core concept combining image processing with machine learning remains 
inherently flexible. Controlled setups in this study helped establish baseline performance metrics and validate the

Conclusion
This study introduces a novel algorithm that couples image processing with machine learning techniques to 
dynamically and efficiently estimate Manning’s n during both the advance and storage phases.
Among the three input scenarios evaluated, the first—combining comprehensive field measurements with 
furrow imagery—achieved the highest prediction accuracy (95–96%). Excluding hydraulic and soil features in 
the second scenario led to a significant drop in classification precision, highlighting the importance of these 
parameters in model accuracy. Scenario III—utilizing images alongside selected field parameters such as inflow 
rate, slope, cross-sectional area, clod index, and irrigation event number—maintained acceptable accuracy with 
only a 3–4% reduction, while reducing field data collection requirements by approximately 80%. This approach 
offers a practical balance between precision and feasibility for real-world applications.
Although the algorithm performed well under controlled imaging conditions (furrows without vegetation, 
fixed camera height and lighting), its generalizability to variable farm environments is constrained. Limitations 
related to vegetative cover, natural lighting variability, and discretized roughness classification may compromise 
model robustness. To address these limitations, future efforts will focus on integrating deep learning architectures 
for illumination-invariant feature extraction and expanding training datasets using diverse imagery captured 
under natural field conditions—ranging from smartphones to DSLR cameras. Moreover, integration with real-
time soil moisture sensors, crop growth models, weather data, and other relevant inputs will enable closed-
loop, adaptive surface irrigation control. While the precise and dynamic estimation of Manning’s n is a critical 
component, its value is magnified when combined with other parameters to support fully adaptive surface 
irrigation platforms. These systems would enable automatic, data-driven water delivery aligned with real-time 
field conditions, maximizing resource efficiency and minimizing waste. This multi-layered integration has 
the potential to enhance scenario-driven irrigation strategies and refine scheduling decisions with field-scale 
precision granularity.

generation irrigation tools. It not only advances research in dynamic hydraulic modeling, but also bridges the
